academic_translation: Subhūti, as for what are called 'virtuous phenomena', the Tathāgata has taught them to be exactly non-phenomena;
translation: Subhuti, the Thus-Gone One has taught that what are called 'good things' are exactly not things.

academic_translation: Therefore, they are called 'virtuous phenomena'.
translation: Therefore, they are called 'good things'.

academic_translation: Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose any son of noble family or daughter of noble family brought together masses of the seven precious substances equal to however many kings of mountains, Mount Sumerus, there are in the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, and gave them as a gift; and suppose someone took up even just a single four-line verse from this perfection of wisdom and taught it to others. Subhūti, that former mass of merit does not come near even a hundredth part of the latter, up to not bearing comparison even as a cause.
translation: Subhuti, think of every world realm in the universe of a billion worlds. Think of every Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, in those worlds. Suppose a son of a good family or a daughter of a good family gathered the seven precious things. Suppose they made a pile as big as all those mountains and gave it all away as a gift. Now suppose someone else learned just one four-line verse from this perfect wisdom. Suppose they taught it to others. Subhuti, that first pile of stored-up goodness does not come close to this new stored-up goodness. It is not even a hundredth part of it. It cannot even be compared.

academic_translation: Subhūti, what do you think?
translation: Subhuti, what do you think?

academic_translation: If you think that the Tathāgata thinks, 'I have liberated sentient beings,' Subhūti, it should not be viewed like that.
translation: If you think the Thus-Gone One thinks, 'I have freed living beings,' Subhuti, you should not see it like that.

academic_translation: Why is that? Because, Subhūti, there are no sentient beings whatsoever who have been liberated by the Tathāgata.
translation: Why is that? Because, Subhuti, there are no living beings at all who have been freed by the Thus-Gone One.

academic_translation: Subhūti, if the Tathāgata were to liberate any sentient being whatsoever, that itself would be grasping at a self by the Tathāgata.
translation: Subhuti, if the Thus-Gone One freed any living being at all, that would mean the Thus-Gone One was clinging to a self.

academic_translation: it would be grasping at a sentient being, grasping at a life-force, and grasping at a person.
translation: It would be clinging to a living being, clinging to a life, and clinging to a person.

academic_translation: Subhūti, as for what is called grasping at a self, the Tathāgata has spoken of it as non-grasping; yet it is grasped by childish ordinary beings.
translation: Subhuti, the Thus-Gone One said that what is called clinging to a self is not clinging. Yet naive ordinary beings still cling to it.

academic_translation: Subhūti, as for what are called childish ordinary beings, the Tathāgata has spoken of them as exactly non-beings;
translation: Subhuti, the Thus-Gone One said that what are called naive ordinary beings are not beings.

academic_translation: therefore they are called childish ordinary beings.
translation: That is why they are called naive ordinary beings.

academic_translation: Subhūti, what do you think?
translation: Subhuti, what do you think?

academic_translation: Do you think that the Tathāgata is to be seen by the perfection of marks?
translation: Do you think the Thus-Gone One is to be seen by perfect marks?

academic_translation: Subhūti replied, Blessed One, it is not so.
translation: Subhuti replied, "Blessed One, it is not so."

academic_translation: The Tathāgata is not to be seen by the perfection of marks.
translation: "You cannot see the Thus-Gone One by perfect marks."

academic_translation: The Blessed One said, Subhūti, it is so. It is just so.
translation: The Blessed One said, "Subhuti, it is so. It is just so."

academic_translation: The Tathāgata is not to be seen by the perfection of marks;
translation: "You cannot see the Thus-Gone One by perfect marks."

academic_translation: Subhūti, if the Tathāgata were to be seen by the perfection of marks, a wheel-turning monarch would also be a Tathāgata.
translation: "Subhuti, if you could see the Thus-Gone One by perfect marks, a wheel-turning king would also be a Thus-Gone One."

academic_translation: Therefore, the Tathāgata is not to be seen by the perfection of marks.
translation: "Therefore, you cannot see the Thus-Gone One by perfect marks."

academic_translation: Then the venerable Subhūti spoke thus to the Blessed One:
translation: Then honored Subhuti said to the Blessed One:

academic_translation: "Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, the Tathāgata is not to be seen by the perfection of marks."
translation: "Blessed One, as I understand what the Blessed One has said, the Thus-Gone One cannot be seen by perfect marks."

academic_translation: Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
translation: Then the Blessed One spoke these verses:

academic_translation: Those who see me as form, those who know me as sound, have entered upon a wrong path;
translation: Those who see me as shape and those who know me as sound have taken a wrong path.

academic_translation: Those people do not see me.
translation: Those people do not see me.

academic_translation: The Buddhas are to be seen as the nature of phenomena.
translation: The Buddhas should be seen as the true nature of things.

academic_translation: The guides are the Dharmakāya. Since the nature of phenomena is not an object to be known, it cannot be cognized.
translation: The guides are the body of the teaching. Since the true nature of things is not an object you can know, it cannot be known.

academic_translation: Subhūti, what do you think?
translation: Subhuti, what do you think?

academic_translation: If you think that the Tathāgata, the arhat, has fully awakened to perfectly complete awakening by means of the perfection of marks, Subhūti, you should not view it like that.
translation: If you think the Thus-Gone One, the worthy one, became fully awake to complete awakening through his perfect marks, Subhuti, you should not see it like that.

academic_translation: Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the arhat, has not fully awakened to perfectly complete awakening by means of the perfection of marks.
translation: Subhuti, the Thus-Gone One, the worthy one, did not become fully awake to complete awakening through his perfect marks.

academic_translation: Subhūti, if you think that those who have correctly entered the bodhisattva vehicle have destroyed some phenomenon or designated it as an annihilation, Subhūti, you should not view it like that.
translation: Subhuti, if you think that those who have truly entered the awakening hero's vehicle have destroyed some thing or called it a cutting off, Subhuti, you should not see it like that.

academic_translation: Those who have correctly entered the bodhisattva vehicle do not designate any phenomenon as destroyed or as an annihilation.
translation: Those who correctly enter the awakening hero's vehicle do not call any thing destroyed or a cutting off.

academic_translation: Moreover, Subhūti, compared to a son of noble family or daughter of noble family who fills world systems as numerous as the sand grains of the Gaṅgā river with the seven precious substances and gives them as a gift, if a bodhisattva attains patience in this Dharma discourse being without self and unborn, he generates from that basis a mass of merit vastly greater, incalculable, and immeasurable.
translation: Also, Subhuti, a son of a good family or a daughter of a good family might fill many world realms with the seven precious things. These realms are as numerous as the sand grains of the Ganges River. They might give them as a gift. But an awakening hero might gain patience in this lesson on the teaching being without a self and not born. From this, they make a pile of stored-up goodness that is vastly greater, countless, and beyond measure.

academic_translation: Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should not take hold of a mass of merit.
translation: Also, Subhuti, an awakening hero should not take hold of a pile of stored-up goodness.

academic_translation: The venerable Subhūti asked, "Blessed One, should a bodhisattva not take hold of a mass of merit?"
translation: The honored Subhuti asked, "Blessed One, should an awakening hero not take hold of a pile of stored-up goodness?"

academic_translation: The Blessed One replied, "Subhūti, one should indeed take hold of it, but one should not take hold of it wrongly;
translation: The Blessed One replied, "Subhuti, one should indeed take hold of it, but one should not take hold of it wrongly.

academic_translation: Therefore, it is called 'taking hold'.
translation: That is why it is called 'taking hold'."

tibetan: ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་འདི་སྐད་དུ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་བཞུད་དམ་བྱོན་ཏམ། བཞེངས་སམ། བཞུགས་སམ། མནལ་བར་མཛད་དོ་ཞེས་ཟེར་ན། དེས་ངས་བཤད་པའི་དོན་མི་ཤེས་སོ། །
academic_translation: Moreover, Subhūti, if anyone were to say, "The Tathāgata goes or comes, stands, sits, or lies down," that person does not understand the meaning of what I have explained.
translation: Also, Subhuti, someone might say, "The Thus-Gone One goes, comes, stands, sits, or lies down." That person does not understand what I have taught.

academic_translation: Why is that? Subhūti, it is because the one called "Tathāgata" has not gone anywhere and has not come from anywhere.
translation: Why is that? Subhuti, the one called the "Thus-Gone One" has not gone anywhere. He has not come from anywhere.

academic_translation: Therefore he is called the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha.
translation: That is why he is called the Thus-Gone One, the worthy one, the complete Buddha.

academic_translation: Moreover, Subhūti, if any son of noble family or daughter of noble family were to grind as many particles of earth as there are in the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system into powder so that they become, for example, like a collection of subtle particles, what do you think, Subhūti, would that collection of subtle particles be numerous?
translation: Moreover, Subhuti, think of a son of a good family or a daughter of a good family. Suppose they ground all the earth in a world realm into powder. Imagine this world realm is a universe of a billion worlds. It would become like a bunch of tiny specks. What do you think, Subhuti? Would that bunch of tiny specks be very large?
